user_message: I've been looking at two growth companies: A and B. Both grew revenue 25% last year but B has a much higher incremental RONIC (return on net incremental capital). Why does that matter?
assistant_message: Because the amount of capital a company has to reinvest to fund the next dollar of growth is inversely related to its incremental return on capital. A high incremental RONIC means each new dollar of growth needs less new capital behind it. The mechanism: incremental ROIC = ΔNOPAT / ΔInvested Capital. So if incremental RONIC > WACC, growth actually creates value; if it's below WACC, growth destroys value even at high revenue growth. Failure conditions to remember: (1) the metric is incremental, not average; (2) accounting distortions can inflate it temporarily; (3) competitive entry compresses it. The reusable principle is: growth × RONIC, not growth alone.
